summary:
"C'est Lunaire !" is an interactive Web app that lets users explore the Moon's South Pole and compare sites for the intersection of sunlight-Earth visibility. Users can select any crater or any point in the map, inspect the terrain in 2D/3D, and move through 30 days of data to see intersection windows.

The App combines NASA's LOLA elevation data with JPL's DE421 ephemerides to compute how lunar terrain and slopes affect sunlight and Earth visibility to determine favorable windows. Interactive charts show when these windows occur and how long they last, regional scan lets users scan nearby optimal windows.

At the lunar South Pole, a terrain ridge can change how much sunlight there is, or whether there is a clear communication path towards Earth. "C'est Lunaire !" gives students, educators and curious explorers and hands-on way to understand how terrain shapes decisions about solar power and potential communications.
details:
"C'est Lunaire !" : A revolutionary way to explore the Moon.

This project is an interactive Web App for exploring the Moon's South Pole and comparing sites for solar illumination and direct Earth visibility. Users can select named craters or any point on the map, inspect it in 2D/3D and a clear factor's analysis inside a user-friendly visibility-luminosity-intersection window display.

HOW DOES IT WORK ?

The App combines NASA LOLA elevation data, Hourly NASA/JPL DE421 ephemerides, and USGS lunar nomenclature. It computes the local terrain horizon in all directions, estimates how much of the Sun's luminosity disk clears the terrain, accounting for angle of sunlight on the slope. It groups consecutive hours when Luminosity is over 10% and Earth's center is visible. Earth visibility serves as a geometric anchor for communication.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACTS :

"C'est Lunaire !" makes clear of how 2 nearby lunar sites can have very different lighting and Earth visibility because of the variable terrain. Curieux Mode guides learners through the basics of the concept, while Enseignant/Chercheur offers site comparison, more thorough data, and CSV/PDF exports. The goal is to make lunar planning concepts accessible to every learning and researching level.

TOOLS AND CREATIVITY :

The app uses HTML, CSS, JS, Three.js for 3D models, and Python for data preparation and local serving. It runs in a standard browser and optimized to run on ordinary hardware. The creative side resides in the possibility of manually exploring lunar landscape (moving with arrows), a time-slider, and charts so users can connect what they see on the terrain to what the integrated engines calculate. A hidden Easter egg : A drivable 3D rover that adds a playful touch to the app ;)

DESIGN CONSIDERATION :

The team tried to balance scientific transparency, browser performance, and accessibility for different audiences. Key design choices reside in : making the assumptions visible, keeping large terrain datasets visible and responsive, supporting keyboard an touch controls, and distinguishing what we see against the computed data.
